fr:title.text: Lifecycle of a JAX program

fr:mainmatter.html:p: We have the following compilation pipeline

html:ol.html:li: Tracing: Python / JAX -> jaxpr

html:ul.html:li: Abstract execution. JAX executes python code using abstract tracer objects instead of real arrays.
Every operation and its intermediate result is recorded into jaxpr.
Sequence used to construct a grap, which the XLA compiler will later optimize.
Python code is executed once during tracing but excluded from final graph.
Each JAX primitive registers functions for
Lowering to StableHLO
How it is transformed under grad and vmap.

html:ol.html:li: Lowering: Jaxpr -> StableHLO

html:ul.html:li: fn_lowered.compiler_ir(dialect='stablehlo') for the MLIR module rather than its text. There is no 'hlo' dialect to ask for here — HLO is produced inside XLA, one step later (chlo desugars, stablehlo is stable, mhlo is internal), and you reach it through .compile().as_text() (Three calls, three IR levels).
Multiple ML frameworks lower to StableHLO.
Hardware agnostic.
Backwards compatible.

html:ol.html:li: Compile: HLO -> Optimized HLO -> LLO IR -> VLIW -> Executables

html:ul.html:li: compiled.runtime_executable() returns a LoadedExecutable.
Useful(?) compiled.cost_analysis().
HLO:
Input for XLA compiler.
Directed acyclic graph of copmutational operations.
All array dimensions are known at compile time.
Limited opcodes i.e. Add, Multiply, Transpose, Dot, etc.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: JAX's trace-level representation: the record of what abstract execution captured when your Python ran once on tracers instead of arrays (Lifecycle of a JAX program). Print one with jax.make_jaxpr(f)(x) (Three calls, three IR levels).

Its defining feature is the square bracket. An equation reads outvars = primitive[static_params] invars, and that bracket is exactly the compile-time / runtime line (Brackets are compile-time, operands are runtime) — everything inside it is baked into this compilation, everything outside flows at run time. The same split appears in MLIR as attributes versus operands (Position separates attributes from regions).

So a jaxpr answers a different class of question from the IR below it. Why is a constant baked in, why did a cast appear (A weak type adopts the other operand's dtype), at what precision is this matmul accumulated (dimension_numbers is contracting then batch), what did my custom gradient rule actually do (A grad jaxpr is the forward program plus its transpose) — none of these survive into optimized HLO, where fusion and layout have already scrambled the correspondence. Read the jaxpr for meaning and the HLO for cost.

Not every JAX transformation appears here. jit, scan, cond, while, and shard_map are primitives with nested jaxprs; vmap is a trace-time rewrite that leaves no trace but the shapes (vmap leaves no primitive behind).

The traces below were produced with JAX 0.11 on CPU. The printed form drifts between releases — scan dropped num_consts for ft_in, and pjit now prints as jit — so read a trace from your own installation before trusting the punctuation in anyone's notes, including these.

html:div.html:p: A whole function. One dense layer, tanh(x @ w + b), traced with jax.make_jaxpr(f)(x, w, b). Four equations, in dependency order, each one a primitive (Brackets are compile-time, operands are runtime):

html:pre.html:code: { lambda ; a:f32[8,16] b:f32[16,4] c:f32[4]. let d:f32[8,4] = dot_general[ dimension_numbers=(([1], [0]), ([], [])) preferred_element_type=float32 ] a b e:f32[1,4] = broadcast_in_dim[broadcast_dimensions=(1,)] c f:f32[8,4] = add d e g:f32[8,4] = tanh f in (g,) }

html:div.html:p: Nothing before the semicolon, so nothing was captured (constvars before the semicolon, invars after). Note what the source did not say: the broadcast of the bias is explicit, and so is the accumulation type on the matmul (dimension_numbers is contracting then batch). Following this same function down to StableHLO and HLO is worth doing once.
A closure. The same trace with w captured from the enclosing scope instead of passed in:

html:pre.html:code: { lambda a:f32[8,4]; b:f32[8]. let c:f32[] = reduce_sum[axes=(0, 1) out_sharding=None] a d:f32[8] = mul b c in (d,) }

html:div.html:p: a is now a constvar, left of the semicolon — baked into this compilation rather than supplied by the caller. A large array on that side of the semicolon is a closure you probably did not mean to make (constvars before the semicolon, invars after).
grad. jax.make_jaxpr(jax.grad(f))(x, w) for f = tanh(x @ w).sum() — the forward pass, then its transpose in reverse order (A grad jaxpr is the forward program plus its transpose):

html:pre.html:code: { lambda ; a:f32[8] b:f32[8,4]. let c:f32[4] = dot_general[dimension_numbers=(([0], [0]), ([], [])) preferred_element_type=float32] a b d:f32[4] = tanh c e:f32[4] = sub 1.0:f32[] d _:f32[] = reduce_sum[axes=(0,) out_sharding=None] d f:f32[4] = broadcast_in_dim 1.0:f32[] g:f32[4] = mul f e h:f32[4] = mul g d i:f32[4] = add_any g h j:f32[8] = dot_general[dimension_numbers=(([0], [1]), ([], [])) preferred_element_type=float32] i b in (j,) }

html:div.html:p: Three things to read off it. The final dot_general contracts [0] against [1] where the forward one contracted [0] against [0] — that swap is the transpose rule for a matmul. The sub 1.0 d is 1 - \tanh ^2 being built from the saved output rather than recomputed. And the reduce_sum is a dropvar (An underscore is an output nobody consumes): the primal value the sum would have produced is not needed, only its gradient, and the cotangent broadcast_in_dim 1.0 is what replaces it.
vmap leaves nothing behind (vmap leaves no primitive behind). Mapping lambda a, b: a * b over the leading axis of a only:

html:pre.html:code: { lambda ; a:f32[3,4] b:f32[4]. let c:f32[1,4] = broadcast_in_dim[broadcast_dimensions=(1,)] b d:f32[3,4] = mul a c in (d,) }

html:div.html:p: There is no vmap equation — only a mul whose avals grew a dimension, plus the broadcast_in_dim that lifted the unmapped argument to match. When vmap can push the batch dimension into an existing primitive it emits nothing at all: jax.vmap(jnp.dot, in_axes=(0, None)) over f32[3,4] and f32[4,2] is a single dot_general, because a batched matvec is a matmul.
scan (consts, then carry, then xs). Two carries, one scanned input, one const closed over:

html:pre.html:code: { lambda ; a:f32[] b:f32[] c:f32[4]. let d:f32[] e:f32[] f:f32[4] = scan[ ft_in=((), (None, None), (None,)) jaxpr={ lambda ; g:f32[] h:f32[] i:f32[]. let j:f32[] = mul g 3.0:f32[] k:f32[] = add j i l:f32[] = add h g m:f32[] = mul g 2.0:f32[] in (k, l, m) } length=4 reverse=False unroll=1 ] a b c in (d, e, f) }

html:div.html:p: Read ft_in first: no consts, two carries, one xs. So invars a and b are the carry and c is scanned, and the body returns two new carries then one ys element, which stacks to f32[4]. The captured 3.0 was constant-folded into the body rather than passed as a const.
cond (The nconsts numbers locate the carry). Note that the predicate is converted to an integer index, and that branch 0 is the false branch:
Both branches take the same operands and return the same type — cond is an n-way switch on an index, and the two-branch boolean case is the special case.
Weak types (A weak type adopts the other operand's dtype). A Python literal against a bf16 array:

html:pre.html:code: { lambda ; a:bf16[3]. let b:bf16[3] = mul a 2.0:bf16[] in (b,) }

html:div.html:p: The literal adopted bf16 and nothing was promoted. Replace 2.0 with np.float32(2.0) — an explicitly typed scalar, so no longer weak — and the same line becomes:

html:pre.html:code: { lambda ; a:bf16[3]. let b:f32[3] = convert_element_type[new_dtype=float32 weak_type=False] a c:f32[3] = mul b 2.0:f32[] in (c,) }

html:div.html:p: The whole array was widened to f32 by one scalar. This is the promotion bug the weak-type rule exists to prevent, and the convert_element_type equation is how you catch it.
shard_map and pmap (Collectives are primitives parameterised by axis name). A psum over a mesh axis of 8:

The global shape is f32[8] and the body's is f32[1] — inside the region you are writing per-device code, which is the whole point of shard_map. pmap is not a separate mechanism: it traces to a jit wrapping a shard_map, with a squeeze and a broadcast_in_dim around the body to move between the mapped axis and the per-device rank.

fr:title.text: Reading one
constvars before the semicolon, invars after

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: constvars before the semicolon, invars after

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Name every part of { lambda a:f32[8] ; b:f32[8] c:f32[8]. let d:f32[8] = mul b c; e:f32[8] = add d a in (e,) }

html:div.html:details:
Answer { lambda <constvars> ; <invars>. let <equations> in (<outvars>) }
Before the semicolon: constvars. Values closed over — captured arrays — supplied by the ClosedJaxpr's consts rather than by the caller.
Between semicolon and dot: invars. The traced arguments.
The let block: equations in dependency order (Brackets are compile-time, operands are runtime).
in (...): the output tuple, always parenthesised even for a single value.
The constvar / invar split is where a performance surprise hides. Anything on the left of the semicolon was captured at trace time and is baked into this compilation, so changing it means retracing (XLA Compilation). Large constvars in a jaxpr you expected to be pure are a closure you did not mean to make.

fr:title.text: Brackets are compile-time, operands are runtime

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Brackets are compile-time, operands are runtime

fr:mainmatter.html:p: What is the shape of a single jaxpr equation?

html:div.html:details:
Answer outvars = primitive[static_params] invars
for example
e:f32[1,4] = broadcast_in_dim[broadcast_dimensions=(1,)] c d:f32[8,4] = dot_general[dimension_numbers=(([1], [0]), ([], [])) preferred_element_type=float32] a b
The square brackets hold static parameters — known at trace time and baked into the primitive — and everything after them is a traced operand or a literal. The printer shows only the interesting ones; the equation carries more (broadcast_in_dim also holds shape and sharding), reachable from eqn.params.
That bracket-versus-operand split is the most useful thing on the page. A quantity inside the brackets is a constant this compilation is specialised to; move it out and you retrace. It is the same distinction MLIR draws between attributes and operands (Position separates attributes from regions).

fr:title.text: An aval is shape and dtype, no value

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: An aval is shape and dtype, no value

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Read the jaxpr shorthand f32[8,128], i32[], bool[3], key<fry>[2], bf16[8]

html:div.html:details:
Answer Compact aval — abstract value — printing: dtype then shape, with empty brackets for a scalar.
key<fry>[2] is a typed PRNG key array using the threefry implementation: the new-style key dtype rather than a raw uint32[2]. Seeing the typed form tells you the key is opaque to shape-manipulating code, which is the point of it.
The aval is what tracing actually propagates: shape, dtype, and Sharding — no values. Everything a jaxpr knows, it knows from these, which is why a Python if on a traced value fails and why the shapes in a jaxpr are always fully static.
HLO's shapes are the same information in a different notation (Tuples are first-class in HLO), and MLIR adds dynamic dimensions that JAX never produces (Question mark is a dynamic dimension, star is unknown rank).

fr:title.text: An underscore is an output nobody consumes

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: An underscore is an output nobody consumes

fr:mainmatter.html:p: What is _:f32[8] on the left of a jaxpr equation?

html:div.html:details:
Answer A dropvar: an output that nothing consumes.
It shows up for multi-output primitives where only some results are used — a custom_vjp's residuals when you asked only for the primal, an unused scan carry (consts, then carry, then xs), the second output of a primitive whose first is all you wanted.
It does not mean the work happens. Dead code elimination may or may not have run when you print a jaxpr, so dropvars are entirely normal in a freshly traced one, and their presence says nothing about the compiled program. XLA will drop the computation if it is genuinely unused.
What they do tell you is which primitive produced more than you asked for — useful when you are trying to work out where a residual came from (A grad jaxpr is the forward program plus its transpose).

fr:title.text: jit is the pjit primitive

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Why does almost every jaxpr from a jitted function contain a single jit[name=f jaxpr={...}] equation?

html:div.html:details:
Answer Because jax.jit is implemented as a primitive — pjit_p, printed as jit — rather than being inlined. The callee's jaxpr is nested inside as a static parameter, so each jit boundary in your code becomes another level of nesting.
That nesting is preserved all the way down. It reappears in HLO as the slash-separated op_name path, jit(f)/jit(g)/... (op_name is the trace path back to Python), which is what lets you attribute an optimized HLO instruction to a particular function in a program full of them.
It also means the boundaries are real to the compiler, not just to you: each is a place where donation, Sharding, and compilation caching are decided (XLA Compilation). Nesting jit inside jit is free at run time but is not invisible in the IR.

fr:title.text: Control flow and collectives
consts, then carry, then xs

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Read scan[ft_in=((), (None, None), (None,)) length=4 reverse=False unroll=1]. How are the invars laid out?

html:div.html:details:
Answer In one fixed order: first the loop-invariant consts, then the carry, then the xs, each scanned along a leading axis of size length. The inner jaxpr's invars follow the same convention, and it returns (new_carry..., ys...).
ft_in is where the split is written down. It is a three-tuple — one group per role — so the group lengths give the counts: none here, then two carries, then one scanned input. Older JAX printed the same information as num_consts and num_carry, and you will still see that form in written material.
Counting is the only way to read a scan body. The names carry nothing; the group sizes do. Given ((), (None, None), (None,)), invars 0 and 1 are the carry and invar 2 is scanned.
The same explicit carry appears as iter_args in scf.for (iter_args and yield are the mutable accumulator) and as a state tuple in HLO's while (A while loop's whole state is one tuple), where the three-way split is flattened into tuple indices you have to recover by counting.

fr:title.text: The nconsts numbers locate the carry

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: The nconsts numbers locate the carry

fr:mainmatter.html:p: How do cond and while print in a jaxpr?

html:div.html:details:
Answer cond[branches=(...)] index a b while[cond_jaxpr={...} cond_nconsts=1 body_jaxpr={...} body_nconsts=2] ...
For cond, the first invar is the branch index and the rest are the operands passed to every branch. branches is a tuple of jaxprs, all with the same signature — which is why both sides of a JAX conditional must agree on shapes and dtypes.
For while, the invars run: cond consts, then body consts, then the carry.
The nconsts numbers are the only thing telling you where the carry starts. There is no punctuation in the operand list and the names are meaningless, so you count: skip cond_nconsts, skip body_nconsts, and everything left is the loop state. Same discipline as scan (consts, then carry, then xs).

fr:title.text: Collectives are primitives parameterised by axis name

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Collectives are primitives parameterised by axis name

fr:mainmatter.html:p: What do psum[axes=('x',) axis_index_groups=None] and shard_map look like in a jaxpr?

html:div.html:details:
Answer Collectives are ordinary primitives parameterised by an axis name; they only mean anything inside a mapped context that binds that name. shard_map appears as
shard_map[jaxpr={...} mesh=Mesh('x': 8, axis_types=(Auto,)) in_specs=(P('x',),) out_specs=(P(),) check_vma=True]
with the per-device program nested inside (vmap leaves no primitive behind). Inside that body a collective whose result is already replicated may print as psum_invariant rather than psum — same reduction, tagged as producing an axis-invariant value.
So the jaxpr level is logical and the physical level is elsewhere. Here you see a named axis and per-device shapes; the device assignment appears only later, as HLO sharding attributes (A sharding annotation is a tiling plus a device order) and concrete all-reduce instructions (replica_groups says who reduces with whom).
That separation is why the axis name is the right thing to reason about: it is stable, whereas which devices land in which replica_groups depends on the mesh and the compiler (Sharding).

fr:title.text: Numerics and transformations
dimension_numbers is contracting then batch

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Read dot_general[dimension_numbers=(((1,), (0,)), ((), ())) precision=None preferred_element_type=float32]

html:div.html:details:
Answer dimension_numbers is ((lhs_contracting, rhs_contracting), (lhs_batch, rhs_batch)) — contracting pair first, batch pair second. Here lhs dim 1 contracts with rhs dim 0 and there are no batch dims: a plain matmul (Batch, contract, free, and the output order is fixed, A dot's output order is batch, lhs free, rhs free).
The two other parameters are where numerics live, and they are easy to skim past.
preferred_element_type is the accumulation type. bf16 inputs accumulating into f32 is the standard configuration, and it is what makes low-precision training work at all — the inputs are cheap, the running sum is not.
precision controls the backend tradeoff: TF32, bf16x3 passes, or full f32.
So a jaxpr answers "at what precision is this matmul actually done" directly, which the HLO line does not.

fr:title.text: A weak type adopts the other operand's dtype

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: A weak type adopts the other operand's dtype

fr:mainmatter.html:p: What does convert_element_type[new_dtype=float32 weak_type=False] mean, and what is a weak type?

html:div.html:details:
Answer An explicit cast that tracing inserted.
weak_type marks a value whose dtype came from a Python scalar — 3.0, 2 — rather than from an explicitly typed array. A weakly typed value adopts the other operand's dtype in promotion instead of forcing a widening, so x * 2.0 on a bf16 array stays bf16 rather than becoming f32.
That rule exists precisely so writing a literal in your model does not silently change its precision.
An unexpected convert_element_type in a jaxpr is therefore worth reading as a diagnosis, not as noise: it is the trace of a promotion you did not intend, usually a NumPy scalar or an f32 constant meeting a lower-precision array. It costs a full pass over the data, and it can defeat the accumulation choice you made on the neighbouring dot_general (dimension_numbers is contracting then batch).

fr:title.text: vmap leaves no primitive behind

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Does vmap appear as a primitive in a jaxpr?

html:div.html:details:
Answer No. Batching is a trace-time rewrite, not a wrapper. The jaxpr you get back has no vmap equation at all — just the same primitives with a batch dimension added to their avals (An aval is shape and dtype, no value), plus extra broadcast_in_dim and transpose equations wherever the batch axis had to be moved.
So to see what vmap decided, read the shapes; there is no op to look for. Those stray transposes are the mapping decisions, and they are also where a vmapped function quietly costs more than the loop you replaced.
Contrast the ones that do appear as primitives with nested jaxprs: pjit (jit is the pjit primitive), scan (consts, then carry, then xs), cond and while (The nconsts numbers locate the carry), custom_jvp_call, and shard_map (Collectives are primitives parameterised by axis name). The distinction is whether the transformation changes the program structure or only the shapes flowing through it.

fr:title.text: A grad jaxpr is the forward program plus its transpose

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: A grad jaxpr is the forward program plus its transpose

fr:mainmatter.html:p: What tells you a jaxpr came from grad?

html:div.html:details:
Answer The layout: the forward equations appear first, then their transposes in reverse order, with residual values threaded between them.
Concrete tells — mul and dot_general with swapped dimension_numbers (dimension_numbers is contracting then batch), transpose equations, and custom_vjp_call_jaxpr or remat wrappers. Dropvars (An underscore is an output nobody consumes) mark residuals that this particular jaxpr does not consume.
jax.make_jaxpr(jax.grad(f))(x) gives the whole forward-plus-backward program as one jaxpr, and that is the cheapest way to see what a custom rule actually did — far cheaper than reasoning about what it should have done. It is also where you can see, directly, which intermediates the backward pass keeps alive, which is the memory question remat exists to answer.
In HLO the same structure is visible through the jvp and transpose scopes in op_name (op_name is the trace path back to Python).

fr:mainmatter.html:p: XLA's internal representation: a directed acyclic graph of tensor operations, with every array dimension known at compile time. It is what StableHLO is converted into on the way into the compiler (chlo desugars, stablehlo is stable, mhlo is internal), and it is not an MLIR dialect — a backend consuming XLA has to translate from HLO on its own (XLA Compilation).

Two design choices shape how an HLO dump reads, and both trade verbosity for locality. Every instruction prints its result shape before the opcode and every operand with its full shape and layout, so a line is self-contained (An HLO line is self-contained); and the module is a flat list of computations rather than a nesting, with ENTRY and ROOT the only structural landmarks (ENTRY names the computation, ROOT names the output). Static shapes are what make the first affordable.

The distinction that matters most in practice is which HLO you are reading. before_optimizations is a transliteration of what JAX emitted; after_optimizations is fused, laid out, and scheduled, and is the only one whose instruction names appear in a profile (Only after_optimizations matches the profile). A performance question answered from the wrong file is answered about a program that never ran.

html:div.html:p: The same function after XLA. jax.jit(f).lower(x, w, b).compile().as_text() for tanh(x @ w + b), on CPU. The two fusion bodies are printed first, then the entry computation:
Read ENTRY first, then follow calls= (ENTRY names the computation, ROOT names the output). The whole program is two kernels. Everything else in the file is their bodies.

html:ul.html:li: Every shape now carries a layout (The layout is minor-to-major), and entry_computation_layout states the ABI the caller must satisfy (The entry layout is the ABI). is_scheduled=true means the order shown is execution order (The gap between start and done is the overlap).

The four jaxpr equations became two kernels, split where the hardware splits. The matmul is kind=kCustom — a library-backed emitter, not generated code — and the bias add and tanh are kind=kLoop, one elementwise pass (The fusion kind names the emitter). The broadcast is inside that loop, so the bias is never materialised to 8x4 in memory (A fusion op is a kernel launch boundary).
A fusion body's parameter(i) lines up with the fusion op's operands (parameter(i) is positional) — that positional match is the only link between body and call site.
The names %add.0 and %add.1 are uniquified junk (The numeric suffix means nothing): %add.1 is a broadcast. Key on metadata instead (op_name is the trace path back to Python).

fr:title.text: Reading a module
An HLO line is self-contained

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Name every part of %add.7 = f32[8,128]{1,0} add(f32[8,128]{1,0} %p0, f32[8,128]{1,0} %bcast.3), metadata={op_name="jit(f)/add"}

html:div.html:details:
Answer %name = <shape> <opcode>(<typed operands>), <attributes>, metadata={...}
Two things differ from MLIR and both are deliberate. The result shape comes before the opcode, and every operand is printed with its full shape and layout (The layout is minor-to-major).
So an HLO line is self-contained. You never scroll up to learn a type — which matters, because an optimized HLO module is one enormous flat list of instructions with no nesting to orient you. The cost is verbosity, and the reason it is affordable is that HLO has no dynamic shapes: every dimension is known at compile time, so every shape can be printed (Question mark is a dynamic dimension, star is unknown rank).
The name is meaningless (The numeric suffix means nothing); metadata is what maps the line back to Python (op_name is the trace path back to Python).

fr:title.text: The layout is minor-to-major

fr:mainmatter.html:p: What does the {1,0} in f32[8,128]{1,0} mean?

html:div.html:details:
Answer The layout: dimension numbers listed minor-to-major. {1,0} says dimension 1 (size 128) is minor-most — the contiguous one — so this is standard row-major. {0,1} on the same shape would be column-major (XLA Compilation).
Layouts appear after XLA's layout assignment pass, so a before_optimizations dump has them but they are not yet meaningful (Only after_optimizations matches the profile).
Layouts are the reason for ops that do nothing mathematically. A copy, bitcast, or transpose that leaves the values unchanged is there to satisfy a layout requirement (bitcast is free, copy is not), typically because a dot wants its contracting dimension minor-most (A dot's output order is batch, lhs free, rhs free) or a custom call pinned one (A custom call is a black box XLA cannot fuse across). Chasing copies in optimized HLO is chasing layout.

fr:title.text: Tuples are first-class in HLO

fr:mainmatter.html:p: What are the HLO shapes s32[], pred[8], (f32[8]{0}, s32[]), and token[]?

html:span.style: font-family: var(--sans); font-size: 11pt; font-weight: 500; color: rgba(0, 0, 0, 0.65);

html:ul.html:li: s32[] — a rank-0 signed 32-bit scalar. The letter is the class: s signed, u unsigned, f float, plus bf16, f8e4m3 and friends for narrow types. Unlike MLIR, HLO integers are signed or unsigned in the type (Signedness lives in the op, not the type).
pred[8] — a boolean array; pred is XLA's bool.

Parens are a tuple shape. Tuples are first-class in HLO, and are how every multi-output op and all while state is expressed (A while loop's whole state is one tuple) — which is why get-tuple-element is everywhere (get-tuple-element is free aliasing).
token[] — an ordering token, carrying no data. Side-effecting ops (infeed, collectives, after-all) thread a token to express an ordering the dataflow graph otherwise could not.

fr:title.text: ENTRY names the computation, ROOT names the output

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: ENTRY names the computation, ROOT names the output

fr:mainmatter.html:p: What do ENTRY and ROOT mark in an HLO module?

html:div.html:details:
Answer ENTRY flags the module's entry computation — the one actually invoked. Every other computation in the file is called by name: fusion bodies (A fusion op is a kernel launch boundary), reducers (reduce removes the dims it lists), while conditions and bodies (A while loop's whole state is one tuple), branch computations.
ROOT flags the single instruction whose value is that computation's output. Every computation has exactly one, and in older dumps it is not necessarily the last line textually.
Why this is the first thing to find. An optimized HLO file is a flat pile of computations in no useful order. ENTRY tells you where the program starts, ROOT tells you where it ends, and following calls= and to_apply= from there is how you read the rest. Its parameter and result shapes must match entry_computation_layout (The entry layout is the ABI).

fr:title.text: The entry layout is the ABI

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: The entry layout is the ABI

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Read the module header HloModule jit_f, entry_computation_layout={(f32[8,128]{1,0}, f32[128]{0})->f32[8,128]{1,0}}, is_scheduled=true

html:div.html:details:
Answer
The module name comes from the jitted function, which is how you tell several compilations apart in a dump directory (The dump filename encodes the stage).
entry_computation_layout is the ABI: the parameter shapes and layouts (The layout is minor-to-major) and the result shape the caller must supply and expect. A buffer whose layout disagrees with this is the mismatch, and it is checked here rather than anywhere friendlier.
is_scheduled=true means this is a post-scheduling dump, so instruction order is actual execution order and not merely a topological sort of the dataflow.
That last flag changes how you read everything below it. Only in a scheduled dump does the distance between an all-reduce-start and its all-reduce-done mean anything (The gap between start and done is the overlap).

fr:title.text: parameter(i) is positional

fr:mainmatter.html:p: What is %p0 = f32[8,128]{1,0} parameter(0), and what does the number mean?

html:div.html:details:
Answer A formal parameter of the enclosing computation. The integer is its position in the parameter list — an index, not a renameable identifier.
Where it points depends on the computation:
In the ENTRY computation (ENTRY names the computation, ROOT names the output), parameter(i) is the i-th argument in entry_computation_layout (The entry layout is the ABI), and so the i-th argument you passed to the jitted function.
In a fusion computation, the parameters correspond positionally to the fusion op's operands (A fusion op is a kernel launch boundary).
That positional correspondence is the thread you pull to read a fusion body. The body names nothing that ties it to the caller — you match parameter(0) to the first operand of the fusion instruction and work inward from there.

fr:title.text: The numeric suffix means nothing

fr:mainmatter.html:p: What does the trailing .7 in %add.7 tell you?

html:div.html:details:
Answer Nothing semantic. It is uniquification of a name that is otherwise derived from the opcode or the metadata — the compiler needed the names distinct and appended a counter.
The numbers change between dumps and between passes, so never key notes, scripts, or diffs on them. Two dumps of the same program with one extra pass in between will renumber wholesale, and a diff on names shows an enormous change where nothing happened.
Key on metadata op_name instead (op_name is the trace path back to Python), which is derived from the JAX trace path and is stable, or on the structure of the graph. The same instability holds for MLIR value names (SSA names are printing hints).

fr:title.text: op_name is the trace path back to Python

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: op_name is the trace path back to Python

fr:mainmatter.html:p: How do you map an HLO instruction back to Python?

html:div.html:details:
Answer The metadata field:
%dot_general.0 = f32[8,4]{1,0} dot(%param_0, %param_1), lhs_contracting_dims={1}, rhs_contracting_dims={0}, metadata={op_name="jit(f)/dot_general" stack_frame_id=2}
op_name is the JAX trace path, not just a label: nested transformation scopes — jit, jvp, transpose, vmap, remat — separated by slashes, ending in the jaxpr primitive that emitted the op.
So it says more than a source line. It says which transformation produced this instruction: an op under jvp(...) is forward-mode work, one under transpose(...) is the backward pass (A grad jaxpr is the forward program plus its transpose).
The source location is indirect. Current XLA interns it: stack_frame_id indexes a StackFrames table printed at the top of the module, which chains through FileLocations to FileNames and FunctionNames. You resolve the id there rather than reading a filename off the instruction, and the chain gives you the whole call stack, not one frame.
This is the path that survives the passes that scramble names (The numeric suffix means nothing). The MLIR equivalent is the location (Locations are the provenance of an op).

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Operator fusion is where XLA earns its keep, and the fusion instruction is the kernel launch boundary — the unit that shows up in a profile and the unit a performance question is usually about.

fr:title.text: A fusion op is a kernel launch boundary

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: A fusion op is a kernel launch boundary

fr:mainmatter.html:p: What is a fusion instruction in HLO and where is its body?

html:div.html:details:
Answer %fusion.2 = f32[8,128]{1,0} fusion(f32[8,128]{1,0} %p0, f32[128]{0} %p1), kind=kLoop, calls=%fused_computation.2
The body is a separate computation named by calls=, printed elsewhere in the module; its parameters line up positionally with the fusion's operands (parameter(i) is positional).
The fusion op is the kernel launch boundary. Everything inside the body runs in one kernel, with intermediates staying in registers instead of round-tripping to High bandwidth memory — that is the whole point of Operator fusion.
It is therefore the unit that matters for performance work: a name in a profile is a fusion name, and the question "why is this slow" is usually "what ended up inside this body, and what did not". kind= says which emitter generated it (The fusion kind names the emitter).

fr:title.text: The fusion kind names the emitter

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: The fusion kind names the emitter

fr:mainmatter.html:p: What do the HLO fusion kinds kLoop, kInput, kOutput, and kCustom mean?

html:div.html:details:
Answer
kLoop — elementwise-style: one loop nest over the output shape, one element per iteration.
kInput — driven by the input iteration space. Used for reductions and transposes, where the operand shape rather than the result shape dictates the loop (reduce removes the dims it lists).
kOutput — fuses producers into an op whose output shape drives the loop, keeping a shared operand live in registers across them.
kCustom — a hand-written emitter or library-backed pattern: a cuDNN or cuBLAS convolution, a Triton emitter.
The kind names the emitter, which is what you actually want when reading a profile. A slow kLoop is a bandwidth question; a slow kInput is usually a reduction whose layout fights its access pattern; a kCustom means the answer is in a library's tuning, not in XLA.

fr:title.text: The opcodes

fr:mainmatter.html:p: A small instruction set whose subtlety lives almost entirely in attributes: which dimensions contract, which are removed, which way a permutation reads. The layout-driven ops repay the closest reading, since they are where a layout mistake surfaces as bandwidth.

fr:title.text: A dot's output order is batch, lhs free, rhs free

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: A dot's output order is batch, lhs free, rhs free

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Read this matmul. %dot.5 = f32[4,8,32]{2,1,0} dot(f32[4,8,16]{2,1,0} %a, f32[4,16,32]{2,1,0} %b), lhs_batch_dims={0}, lhs_contracting_dims={2}, rhs_batch_dims={0}, rhs_contracting_dims={1}

html:div.html:details:
Answer Batch dimensions pair up and are preserved, contracting dimensions pair up and are summed away, and everything left over is free — the same three-way split as StableHLO (Batch, contract, free, and the output order is fixed) and jaxpr (dimension_numbers is contracting then batch).
The output order is always batch, then lhs free in order, then rhs free in order, giving [4, 8, 32] here. You never choose it.
Then read the layouts, because that is where the performance question lives. If a contracting dimension is not minor-most for its operand's layout (The layout is minor-to-major), the data has to be moved before the Matrix Multiply Unit (MXU) or tensor core can consume it — so expect a transpose or copy next to the dot (bitcast is free, copy is not), and expect it to cost real bandwidth.

fr:title.text: dim_labels spells out three layouts

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Read the convolution annotations window={size=3x3 stride=2x2 pad=1_1x1_1}, dim_labels=b01f_01io->b01f

html:div.html:details:
Answer window describes the spatial sweep: the window size, the stride, and per-dimension padding written low_high. So pad=1_1x1_1 is one before and one after in each of two spatial dimensions. The field can also carry lhs_dilate and rhs_dilate, which is how transposed and atrous convolutions are expressed rather than as separate opcodes.
dim_labels gives three layouts at once, as input_kernel->output, with b batch, f feature, i input feature, o output feature, and digits for spatial dimensions.
So b01f_01io->b01f is an NHWC input, an HWIO kernel, and an NHWC output. These are logical dimension roles, distinct from the physical minor-to-major layout (The layout is minor-to-major) — and a mismatch between the two is the usual reason a transpose appears beside a convolution.

fr:title.text: broadcast dimensions read operand to output

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: broadcast dimensions read operand to output

fr:mainmatter.html:p: In %b = f32[2,3]{1,0} broadcast(f32[3]{0} %a), dimensions={1}, what does dimensions mean?

html:div.html:details:
Answer For each operand dimension in order, which output dimension it maps to. Operand dim 0 lands at output dim 1; output dimensions not mentioned are the newly broadcast ones.
This is the same convention as stablehlo.broadcast_in_dim (broadcast_in_dim maps operand dims onto output dims), which is what it lowers from.
Note that it reads the opposite way from transpose (transpose dimensions read output from operand), which lists a source dimension per output position. Both attributes are a list of integers on an op that rearranges dimensions, and confusing them is the single easiest mistake to make in an HLO dump. The tell is length: a broadcast's list has the operand's rank, a transpose's has the output's.

fr:title.text: transpose dimensions read output from operand

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: transpose dimensions read output from operand

fr:mainmatter.html:p: In transpose(%a), dimensions={1,0,2}, which way does the permutation go?

html:div.html:details:
Answer Output dimension i takes operand dimension dimensions[i]. So output dim 0 is operand dim 1 — you read a source per output position, the opposite direction from broadcast (broadcast dimensions read operand to output).
Then check whether it moves any data. If the permutation is a no-op given the operands' layouts (The layout is minor-to-major) — the bytes are already in the order the result wants — XLA rewrites it to a bitcast, which is free. A permutation that genuinely reorders bytes stays a transpose or becomes a copy, and costs a full read and write of the array (bitcast is free, copy is not).
So a transpose in optimized HLO is worth a second look: either it vanished into a bitcast, or someone is paying for it.

fr:title.text: reduce removes the dims it lists

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: reduce removes the dims it lists

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Read %r = f32[8]{0} reduce(f32[8,128]{1,0} %a, f32[] %zero), dimensions={1}, to_apply=%add_computation

html:div.html:details:
Answer dimensions lists the dimensions that are removed. The second operand is the init value — the identity of the reducer, and the answer for an empty reduction. to_apply names a computation of two scalars to one scalar, so reductions are user-defined rather than drawn from a fixed list (reduce takes a computation, not an enum).
Variadic reduce is the part worth knowing. It takes several operand and init pairs and returns a tuple (Tuples are first-class in HLO), with the reducer taking and yielding one scalar per pair. That is how argmax is expressed — reduce the values and the indices together, with a reducer that compares on the value and carries the index — and likewise a fused mean-and-variance.
So a reduce with a tuple result is not multiple reductions; it is one pass whose accumulator has several fields.

fr:title.text: bitcast is free, copy is not

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: bitcast is free, copy is not

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Distinguish HLO's reshape, bitcast, and copy.

html:div.html:details:
Answer
reshape — a logical shape change. Whether it costs anything depends on the layouts (The layout is minor-to-major) on either side; before layout assignment you cannot yet tell.
bitcast — free reinterpretation: the same bytes, a different shape or layout. Emitted after layout assignment, once the compiler has proved no movement is needed. Costs nothing at run time.
copy — real data movement, almost always to satisfy a layout or memory-space requirement.
So the three are a progression, not three ways of saying the same thing: a reshape resolves into a bitcast if the layouts cooperate and a copy if they do not.
Many copies in optimized HLO is a layout problem worth chasing — usually a dot (A dot's output order is batch, lhs free, rhs free) or a custom call (A custom call is a black box XLA cannot fuse across) that pinned a layout the rest of the program does not want.

fr:title.text: get-tuple-element is free aliasing

fr:mainmatter.html:p: What is %gte.1 = f32[8]{0} get-tuple-element(%t), index=0, and why is it everywhere?

html:div.html:details:
Answer It extracts one element of a tuple value. Tuples are how HLO returns more than one thing (Tuples are first-class in HLO), so every multi-output op is followed by a fan of these: while (A while loop's whole state is one tuple), a fusion with several outputs, a custom call, sort, variadic reduce (reduce removes the dims it lists).
They are free at run time — pure aliasing into the tuple's buffers, no data moves.
So read them as punctuation, not as work. A while body that is half get-tuple-element at the top and tuple at the bottom is not doing anything; it is unpacking and repacking the carry. MLIR avoids the whole idiom by giving ops multiple results natively (A multi-result op binds one name and indexes into it).

fr:title.text: A while loop's whole state is one tuple

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: A while loop's whole state is one tuple

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Read %w = (s32[], f32[8]{0}) while(%init), condition=%cond, body=%body

html:div.html:details:
Answer A loop whose entire state is one tuple value. %cond is a computation from that tuple to pred[]; %body is a computation from the tuple to the same tuple.
Trip counters, carried values, and the arrays being scanned are all packed into that one tuple, which is why loop bodies are full of get-tuple-element and tuple pairs (get-tuple-element is free aliasing) — the body has to unpack the state, work, and repack it.
This is what jax.lax.scan and fori_loop lower to (consts, then carry, then xs), and the packing is where their structure gets lost: the jaxpr's clean split into consts, carry, and xs becomes tuple indices you have to recover by counting. Read the jaxpr first when you want to know what the loop means, and the HLO when you want to know what it costs.

fr:title.text: dynamic-slice clamps instead of failing

fr:mainmatter.html:p: What is the clamping rule for dynamic-slice(%operand, %i0, %i1), dynamic_slice_sizes={1,128}?

html:div.html:details:
Answer The start indices are scalar operands, one per dimension, and they are clamped so the whole slice stays in bounds:
\text {start} = \mathrm {clamp}(\text {index},\; 0,\; \text {dim size} - \text {slice size})
There is no out-of-bounds error — you silently get a shifted slice. That is a deliberate choice: on an accelerator there is nowhere to raise from, so the semantics are total. It is also why an off-by-one in indexing code produces plausible wrong numbers rather than a crash.
The sizes must be compile-time constants, since the result shape is part of the type (An HLO line is self-contained) — which is why genuinely dynamic shapes need a different construct entirely.
Its dual is dynamic-update-slice, the basis of every in-place buffer update and what x.at[i].set(v) becomes.

fr:title.text: iota builds indices without a constant

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: iota builds indices without a constant

fr:mainmatter.html:p: What do iota(), iota_dimension=1 and constant({...}) do in HLO?

html:div.html:details:
Answer iota generates 0, 1, 2, \ldots along the given dimension and is constant across the others. It is how arange, index comparisons, and position-dependent masks appear — a causal attention mask is an iota on rows compared against an iota on columns.
The point is that it materialises nothing. A mask built from iota is computed inside the consuming kernel, so it fuses (A fusion op is a kernel launch boundary) and never occupies High bandwidth memory. The same mask written as a literal would be a constant the size of the attention matrix, read from memory every step.
constant embeds a literal, and a large one is elided in the text dump as {...} — present in the module, dropped from the printout, the same courtesy MLIR extends with dense_resource (A scalar inside dense is a splat).

fr:title.text: A custom call is a black box XLA cannot fuse across

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: A custom call is a black box XLA cannot fuse across

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Read custom-call(%a, %b), custom_call_target="tpu_custom_call", operand_layout_constraints={...}, backend_config="...", api_version=API_VERSION_STATUS_RETURNING

html:div.html:details:
Answer The escape hatch to code XLA does not generate: library kernels (cuBLAS, cuDNN), Pallas and Mosaic or Triton kernels (A Pallas kernel is an opaque custom call), host callbacks.
custom_call_target selects the registered handler by name.
backend_config carries the opaque payload — a serialised Mosaic module, a tuning configuration, an algorithm choice.
operand_layout_constraints pins the layouts the handler requires (The layout is minor-to-major).
Everything expensive about a custom call follows from XLA not being able to see inside it. It cannot fuse across the boundary, so the operands are materialised to High bandwidth memory and the results read back; it must assume the declared effects, so it cannot reorder freely; and the pinned layouts can force copy ops on both sides (bitcast is free, copy is not).
A hand-written kernel has to beat all of that, not just the kernel XLA would have emitted.

fr:title.text: Collectives and sharding

fr:mainmatter.html:p: On a sharded program the instructions worth reading are the ones that move bytes between chips. Collectives summary covers what they compute; these cover how to read them out of a dump, and how to tell whether the scheduler overlapped them with anything.

fr:title.text: replica_groups says who reduces with whom

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: replica_groups says who reduces with whom

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Read all-reduce(%a), replica_groups={{0,1},{2,3}}, to_apply=%add, channel_id=1, use_global_device_ids=true

html:div.html:details:
Answer
replica_groups — which devices reduce together. Each inner list is an independent group, so this is two separate AllReduces of two devices, not one of four.
to_apply — the combiner computation (reduce removes the dims it lists): sum, max, and so on.
channel_id present means cross-partition (SPMD, Sharding) rather than pure cross-replica; with use_global_device_ids the numbers in replica_groups are global device ids rather than per-replica ones.
Read the group structure before the opcode: it tells you which mesh axis this collective runs on, and therefore whether it crosses ICI or the slower host network.
The family is Collectives summary: AllGather (with dimensions= naming the concatenation axis), ReduceScatter, all-to-all, and collective-permute with source_target_pairs={{0,1},{1,0}}.

fr:title.text: The gap between start and done is the overlap

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: The gap between start and done is the overlap

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Why do you see all-reduce-start / all-reduce-done pairs (and copy-start / copy-done, async-start / async-done)?

html:div.html:details:
Answer Asynchronous decomposition, so the operation can overlap with compute. start issues it and returns a handle — a tuple of buffers and context (Tuples are first-class in HLO) — and done waits and yields the result. The scheduler is then free to place independent work between them.
The distance between the pair is the measurement. In a scheduled dump (is_scheduled=true, The entry layout is the ABI) instruction order is execution order, so an adjacent start and done means the compiler found nothing to overlap and you are paying the full collective latency in serial.
That is the cheapest read on whether a sharded model is communication-bound: not the presence of AllReduce (replica_groups says who reduces with whom), which is expected, but how much compute the scheduler managed to slide underneath it.

fr:title.text: A sharding annotation is a tiling plus a device order

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: A sharding annotation is a tiling plus a device order

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Decode sharding={replicated}, sharding={devices=[2,4]<=[8]}, sharding={devices=[2,4]<=[4,2]T(1,0)}, sharding={maximal device=0}

html:div.html:details:
Answer
replicated — a full copy on every device.
devices=[2,4] — the tensor is tiled two ways on dim 0 and four ways on dim 1. The <=[8] is shorthand for the device list being iota over eight devices.
<=[4,2]T(1,0) — that iota device list is reshaped to [4,2] and transposed before being laid over the tiles. Same tiling, different device-to-tile assignment.
maximal device=0 — computed on exactly one device.
The device order is not cosmetic. It decides which mesh axis is "fast" — whether neighbouring tiles sit on neighbouring chips over ICI or across a slower hop — so two Sharding annotations with identical tilings can differ by a large factor in collective cost (replica_groups says who reduces with whom).
A trailing last_tile_dim_replicate means the final tile dimension is replication rather than data.

fr:title.text: XLA Compilation

html:ul.html:li: Dispatch / Cache: caches compilation based on input argument signatures i.e. shapes, dtypes, sharding. If shapes change will need to recompile.

Lowering: Python -> jaxpr -> StableHLO. This stage is a translation, not an optimization — no Operator fusion happens here. See chlo desugars, stablehlo is stable, mhlo is internal for the dialects involved and Three calls, three IR levels for how to print each level.

XLA: StableHLO is converted to HLO, and the optimizing passes — simplification, layout assignment, fusion, collective scheduling, memory assignment — run there. Read after_optimizations, not before_optimizations, for anything performance-related (Only after_optimizations matches the profile).
TPU specific: Further reduced to LLO IR, then very large instruction word (VLIW) scheduling to map dot products to Matrix Multiply Unit (MXU).

fr:mainmatter.html:div: Remark. The Python source is thrown away as soon as it is traced into a jaxpr, and the jaxpr in turn is thrown away once it is lowered. What XLA ingests is StableHLO, which it converts to HLO before optimizing; HLO is XLA's internal representation, not its input format. The only thread back to the Python you wrote is the metadata carried on each instruction (op_name is the trace path back to Python).

fr:title.text: Getting the dumps

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Half of reading compiler output is arranging to read the right compiler output. The recurring mistake is answering a performance question from before_optimizations, which describes a program that never ran.

fr:title.text: Three calls, three IR levels

fr:mainmatter.html:p: How do you print each IR level for a JAX function f?

html:div.html:details:
Answer
jaxpr — jax.make_jaxpr(f)(x).
StableHLO, pre-XLA — jax.jit(f).lower(x).as_text(), or .compiler_ir(dialect='stablehlo').
Optimized HLO, post-XLA passes and matching the profile — jax.jit(f).lower(x).compile().as_text().
The three answer genuinely different questions, and reaching for the wrong one wastes an afternoon (Lifecycle of a JAX program):
The jaxpr says what tracing captured — so it answers "why is this constant baked in", "why is there a convert_element_type here" (A weak type adopts the other operand's dtype), "did my Python branch get traced at all".
The StableHLO says what JAX handed to XLA — the boundary where a JAX bug becomes an XLA bug.
The optimized HLO says what XLA built — fusions, layouts, collectives (Only after_optimizations matches the profile).

fr:title.text: Only after_optimizations matches the profile

fr:mainmatter.html:p: What is the difference between the before_optimizations and after_optimizations HLO files in an XLA dump?

html:div.html:details:
Answer before_optimizations — the HLO as imported from StableHLO. Shapes carry no meaningful layouts yet (The layout is minor-to-major), nothing is fused, and there is roughly one instruction per source operation. Read it when you want to know what JAX asked for.
after_optimizations — past simplification, layout assignment, Operator fusion, collective scheduling, and memory assignment. Read it when you want to know what runs.
Only the second one corresponds to the kernels in a profile, because the fusion names in the profile are the fusion instruction names here (A fusion op is a kernel launch boundary). A performance question answered from before_optimizations is answered about a program that never executed — the op you are worried about may have been fused away, folded, or duplicated (The dump filename encodes the stage).

fr:title.text: Per-pass dumps find the pass that broke it

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Per-pass dumps find the pass that broke it

fr:mainmatter.html:p: What does XLA_FLAGS=--xla_dump_to=/tmp/dump give you, and how do you get per-pass IR?

html:div.html:details:
Answer A directory of per-module files: pre- and post-optimization HLO text (Only after_optimizations matches the profile), the buffer assignment, and on GPU the generated PTX and LLVM IR (The dump filename encodes the stage).
Add --xla_dump_hlo_pass_re=.* to dump the HLO before and after every pass matching the regex. That is how you find which pass introduced a copy or broke a fusion — bisect the pass list rather than staring at the endpoints. Narrow the regex once you have a suspect, since .* on a real model produces a great many files.
--xla_dump_hlo_as_html and --xla_dump_hlo_as_dot give graph views, which are far easier than text for fusion structure (A fusion op is a kernel launch boundary) — a flat instruction list hides exactly the thing you are looking at.
The MLIR side has the same facility in --mlir-print-ir-after-all (Print generic, print locations, disable threading).

fr:title.text: The dump filename encodes the stage

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: The dump filename encodes the stage

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Reading an XLA dump directory: what is in module_0001.jit_f.before_optimizations.txt versus the after_optimizations and sm_XX files?

html:div.html:details:
Answer The filename encodes module index, entry name, and pipeline stage. Read them in this order:
before_optimizations — one-to-one with your StableHLO. Use it to confirm JAX emitted what you meant.
after_optimizations — fused, laid out, scheduled. Map profile kernels to the fusion names here (Only after_optimizations matches the profile).
Backend artifacts — PTX and LLVM IR on GPU, Mosaic or LLO on TPU. What actually ran.
Each module index is a separate compilation, so a program with several jit boundaries, or one that retraced on a new input shape, produces several sets. When a dump directory has more modules than you expected, that count is the finding — it means recompilation you did not intend (XLA Compilation).

Unlike a Markov chain, in addition to the hidden states, a hidden markov models contains observations x \in \mathcal {X} with associated emission probabilities \mathbb {P}(x_t \mid h_t).

fr:title.text: Flash Attention (v1)

fr:mainmatter.html:p: This will be a brief tour through all the fundamentals needed to understand the first instantiation of FlashAttention as introduced in FlashAttention: Fast and Memory-Efficient Exact Attention with IO-Awareness.

fr:title.text: Online Softmax

fr:mainmatter.html:p: This covers the math behind the online softmax algorithm required by Flash Attention (v1).

fr:title.text: Safe softmax

fr:mainmatter.html:p: The first thing we must consider is numerical precision. Namely, the original softmax operation is given by
However, when operating with low precision data types (i.e. float16) the maximum value is 65536. Therefore, with \exp we can easily get numerically overflow.

To get around this, the online softmax algorithm adheres to the safe softmax. For safe softmax, we simply multiply the numerator and denominator by \exp (-m), where m = \max \{x_{1}, \ldots , x_n\}. This gives
Since x_i - m \leq 0, this ensures that each \exp (x_i - m) is bounded in a safe range.
fr:mainmatter.html:div: Problem. Note that computing the \max over \mathbf {x} means that we must have all of the logits in a row of QK^T materialized in SMEM, or first loop over all of them to compute the max before computing the normalization constant.

fr:title.text: Fusing the max and normalization

fr:mainmatter.html:p: The online softmax algorithm fuses the max reduction into the normalization pass, so a single sweep over the row suffices to compute the normalization with the max. The key difficulty is that the denominator depends on n for each i i.e.

Therefore, we must find a recursive relationship such that d_{i+1} = f(d_i, m_i, x_{i+1}) for some function f. This would then allow us to locally compute d_{i+1} with only the local information of current x_{i+1} and the two running statistics d_i and m_i. This is exactly the kind of algorithm that is conducive to memory tiling.
fr:mainmatter.html:div: Question. What is f(d_i, m_i, x_{i+1})?

html:div.html:details: Answer.Consider d_{i+1} = d_i \cdot \exp (m_{i} - m_{i + 1}) + \exp (x_{i + 1} - m_{i + 1}).

Proof. This can be seen by directly rewriting d_{i + 1}.
\begin {align*} d_{i + 1} &= \sum _{j = 1}^{i+1} \exp (x_j - m_{i + 1}) \\ &= \left (\sum _{j = 1}^{i} \exp (x_j - m_{i+1})\right ) + \exp (x_{i+1} - m_{i+1}) \\ &= \left (\sum _{j = 1}^{i} \exp (x_j - m_{i})\right )\exp (m_{i} - m_{i + 1}) + \exp (x_{i+1} - m_{i+1}) \\ &= d_{i} \exp (m_{i} - m_{i + 1}) + \exp (x_{i+1} - m_{i+1}) \end {align*}

fr:mainmatter.html:p: The running denominator d is rescaled by e^{m - m_{\text {new}}} each time a new maximum is found, keeping it consistent with the safe-softmax shift.

html:pre.html:code: m = float("-inf") # running max of the logits d = 0.0 # running softmax denominator for i in range(n): # one fused sweep for the stats m_new = max(m, x[i]) d = d * exp(m - m_new) + exp(x[i] - m_new) m = m_new p = [exp(x[i] - m) / d for i in range(n)] # second pass: normalized probs

fr:mainmatter.html:div: Remark. Unfortunately, we cannot get around the second pass to compute the normalized output for \mathbf {p}. However, this is not the case in Flash Attention (v1).

fr:title.text: Flash Attention (Fwd)

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Unlike in the online softmax, we are not interested in the outputted probability vector \mathbf {p}. Instead we are interested in the entire output matrix O given by
For more details see self-attention.
fr:mainmatter.html:div: Notation. In correspondence with the notation in the online softmax, we define the following: x_{i,j} = \mathbf {q}_i \cdot \mathbf {k}_j, where \mathbf {q}_i is the ith row of Q and \mathbf {k}_j is the jth row of K. Similarly, \mathbf {o}_i is the ith row of the output matrix O given by \mathbf {o}_i = \sum _{j = 1}^{n} \frac {\exp (x_{i,j} - m_n)}{d_n} \cdot \mathbf {v}_j
fr:mainmatter.html:p: Now following the template provided by the online softmax, we must find a recurrence for \mathbf {o}_i. Namely, we will consider the sequence \mathbf {o}_{i,k}' given by \mathbf {o}_{i,k}' = \sum _{j = 1}^{k} \frac {\exp (x_{i,j} - m_k)}{d_k} \cdot \mathbf {v}_j, such that \mathbf {o}_{i,n}' = \mathbf {o}_n
fr:mainmatter.html:div:
Claim. We have the following recurrence for \mathbf {o}_{i,k}':
\mathbf {o}_{i,k}' = \mathbf {o}_{i, k-1} \cdot \frac {d_{k - 1} \cdot \exp (m_{k-1} - m_{k})}{d_k} + \frac {\exp (x_{i,j} - m_k)}{d_k} \cdot \mathbf {v}_k

html:div.html:details:
Proof. We will proceed by directly rewriting the recurrence for \mathbf {o}_{i,k}' as
\begin {align*} \mathbf {o}_{i,k}' &= \sum _{j = 1}^{k} \frac {\exp (x_{i,j} - m_k)}{d_k} \cdot \mathbf {v}_j \\ &= \left (\sum _{j = 1}^{k - 1} \frac {\exp (x_{i,j} - m_{k-1})}{d_{k-1}} \cdot \mathbf {v}_j\right ) \frac {d_{k - 1} \cdot \exp (m_{k-1} - m_{k})}{d_k} + \frac {\exp (x_{i,k} - m_k)}{d_k} \cdot \mathbf {v}_k \\ &= \mathbf {o}_{i, k-1} \cdot \frac {d_{k - 1} \cdot \exp (m_{k-1} - m_{k})}{d_k} + \frac {\exp (x_{i,k} - m_k)}{d_k} \cdot \mathbf {v}_k .\end {align*}

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Thus, we are left with the following algorithm

html:pre.html:code: for i in range(N): # one query row at a time m = float("-inf") # running max of the logits d = 0.0 # running softmax denominator o = zeros(head_dim) # running output accumulator for j in range(M): # stream over keys/values x = q[i] @ k[j] # logit x_{i,j} m_new = max(m, x) d_new = d * exp(m - m_new) + exp(x - m_new) o = o * (d * exp(m - m_new) / d_new) + (exp(x - m_new) / d_new) * v[j] m, d = m_new, d_new out[i] = o

fr:mainmatter.html:div: Remark. A key benefit of this algorithm is that it is entirely parallelizable across rows. This means that we can loop across entire tiles like in the GEMM case.

fr:title.text: Flash Attention (Bwd)

fr:mainmatter.html:p: The forward pass of flash attention avoids materializing the N \times N attention matrix by streaming an online softmax. The backward pass has to pull the same trick twice over, because the naive gradient computation wants two N \times N matrices — \mathbf {P} and d\mathbf {P}. Getting there means first writing down every gradient we need, then finding a way to recompute rather than store each one.
fr:mainmatter.html:div: Notation. Following the notation in the original paper, \mathbf {S} = \mathbf {Q} \mathbf {K}^T, \quad \mathbf {P} = \mathrm {softmax}(\mathbf {S}), \quad \mathbf {O} = \mathbf {P} \mathbf {V}, where \mathbf {Q}, \mathbf {K}, \mathbf {V}, \mathbf {O} are N \times d and \mathbf {S}, \mathbf {P} are N \times N. For a scalar loss \phi we abbreviate the gradient with respect to any matrix \mathbf {X} as d\mathbf {X} = \frac {\partial \phi }{\partial \mathbf {X}}, and write \mathbf {L}_i for the softmax denominator of row i saved by the forward pass, so that \mathbf {P}_{ij} = \exp (\mathbf {Q}_i \cdot \mathbf {K}_j) / \mathbf {L}_i.

fr:title.text: The gradients we need for FlashAttention

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: The gradients we need for FlashAttention

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Everything downstream is chain rule; the only step with any content is differentiating through the softmax. We take the gradients in dependency order, starting from d\mathbf {O} which arrives from the layer above.

fr:title.text: d\mathbf {P} and d\mathbf {V} from \mathbf {O} = \mathbf {P}\mathbf {V}

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Both fall straight out of the product rule for matrices:

The shapes are a useful sanity check. d\mathbf {O} has one entry per output, so it is N \times d; \mathbf {V}^T is d \times N; their product is N \times N, matching \mathbf {P}. Likewise \mathbf {P}^T d\mathbf {O} is N \times d, matching \mathbf {V}.
Componentwise, from \mathbf {O}_{ik} = \sum _j \mathbf {P}_{ij} \mathbf {V}_{jk},
That last line is worth noting already: d\mathbf {V} never needs \mathbf {P} stored, only the ability to re-evaluate \mathbf {P}_{ij} from \mathbf {Q}, \mathbf {K}, and \mathbf {L}.

fr:title.text: d\mathbf {S} through the softmax

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Softmax acts row by row, so drop into the scalar case with \mathbf {s} and \mathbf {p} single rows. The softmax Jacobian is \partial \mathbf {p}_i / \partial \mathbf {s}_j = \mathbf {p}_i(\delta _{ij} - \mathbf {p}_j), giving

As a row vector this is d\mathbf {s} = \mathbf {p} \odot (d\mathbf {p} - \mathbf {p} \cdot d\mathbf {p}), where the subtracted term is the scalar \mathbf {p} \cdot d\mathbf {p} broadcast across the row. Collecting those scalars into a column \mathbf {D} with \mathbf {D}_i = \mathbf {P}_i \cdot d\mathbf {P}_i recovers the matrix form
\mathbf {D} is the piece that will cause trouble later: it is a dot product over an entire row of \mathbf {P}, which is exactly the thing we refuse to materialize.

fr:title.text: d\mathbf {Q} and d\mathbf {K} from \mathbf {S} = \mathbf {Q}\mathbf {K}^T

fr:mainmatter.html:p: One more chain rule, and the sums run over opposite indices:

fr:title.text: Recomputing instead of storing

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Every gradient above is expressed through \mathbf {P}_{ij} and d\mathbf {P}_{ij}, both N \times N. Materializing either one is exactly the quadratic memory cost the forward pass went to such lengths to avoid, so the backward pass has to be able to produce those entries on demand.
fr:mainmatter.html:div: Insight. Both are recoverable from the N \times d tensors already resident in memory. The forward pass saved \mathbf {L}, so \mathbf {P}_{ij} = \frac {\exp \left (\mathbf {Q}_{i} \cdot \mathbf {K}_{j}\right )}{\mathbf {L}_{i}}, and d\mathbf {P} is just an inner product of two rows, d\mathbf {P}_{ij} = \sum _{k} d\mathbf {O}_{ik} \mathbf {V}_{jk} = d\mathbf {O}_{i} \cdot \mathbf {V}_j. Neither ever requires an N \times N intermediate.
fr:mainmatter.html:p: Substituting both into the previous section leaves d\mathbf {Q} and d\mathbf {K} in terms of \mathbf {Q}, \mathbf {K}, \mathbf {V}, d\mathbf {O}, \mathbf {L}, and \mathbf {D} alone:

fr:title.text: Getting \mathbf {D} for free

fr:mainmatter.html:p: One problem survives. \mathbf {D}_i = \mathbf {P}_i \cdot d\mathbf {P}_i is a dot product over a full row, so computing it inside the streaming loop would mean a reduction over all j before any tile of d\mathbf {Q}_i could be finished. This is the same global dependency the online softmax was designed to break.
The way out is that the row sum has already been computed once, in the forward pass. Expanding and pulling d\mathbf {O}_i out of the sum:

The inner sum is precisely the definition of \mathbf {O}_i. So \mathbf {D} is a single elementwise product of d\mathbf {O} and \mathbf {O} summed along the head dimension — one O(Nd) pass over tensors we already have, done once before the backward loop begins.
Forward pass. Store \mathbf {O} and the softmax denominators \mathbf {L}, both O(Nd).
Between the passes. Receive d\mathbf {O} from the layer above (automatic in JAX), then precompute \mathbf {D}_i = d\mathbf {O}_i \cdot \mathbf {O}_i in O(N) memory.
Backward pass. Stream over tiles, recomputing \mathbf {P}_{ij} from \mathbf {Q}, \mathbf {K}, \mathbf {L} and d\mathbf {P}_{ij} from d\mathbf {O}, \mathbf {V} as needed:

html:ol.html:li: d\mathbf {V}_j = \sum _i \mathbf {P}_{ij} d\mathbf {O}_i, accumulated over query tiles.
d\mathbf {Q}_i = \sum _j \mathbf {P}_{ij}(d\mathbf {O}_i \cdot \mathbf {V}_j - \mathbf {D}_i)\mathbf {K}_j, accumulated over key tiles.
d\mathbf {K}_j = \sum _i \mathbf {P}_{ij}(d\mathbf {O}_i \cdot \mathbf {V}_j - \mathbf {D}_i)\mathbf {Q}_i, accumulated over query tiles.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Each accumulator is O(d) per row or column, so the whole backward pass stays linear in N.

fr:title.text: The running max makes the chunk merge exact

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: The running max makes the chunk merge exact

fr:mainmatter.html:p: In flash attention, what running statistics travel between KV chunks, and how are two chunks merged?

html:div.html:details:
Answer Each query block carries three: M, the running maximum of q \cdot k; L, the running softmax denominator; and O, the running output.
Merging chunks with local maxima M^1, M^2 and sums L^1, L^2 rescales each to the shared maximum:
L = e^{M^1 - \max (M^1, M^2)}L^1 + e^{M^2 - \max (M^1, M^2)}L^2
This is exact, not an approximation. It is only \sum _i e^{a_i + b} = e^b \sum _i e^{a_i}: pulling a constant out of a sum of exponentials. The maximum is subtracted for numerical stability and put back by the same identity — see Online Softmax for the one-pass version of the argument.
The payoff is memory, not FLOPs. The [B,T,S,N] attention matrix is never materialised, so memory is O(1) in the number of chunks while the FLOP count stays quadratic. The query block sits in VMEM and only the KV chunks stream in, which is also what raises the arithmetic intensity.

fr:title.text: Implementing Directory-based MESI in Murphi

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Murphi is an explicit-state model checker: you describe a system as guarded transition rules, state the invariants, and it enumerates every reachable interleaving looking for a violation. That makes it a natural fit for cache coherence, where the steady-state behavior is easy and the races are not. This post builds a directory-based MESI protocol in Murphi, starting from MSI and adding state every time the checker finds a way to break it.

The state tables come from A Primer on Memory Consistency and Cache Coherence, which doubles as the source for these notes. The recurring lesson is that the published tables are not quite enough: every protocol below needs transient states the tables leave implicit.
Syntactical things I need to remember from Murphi docs. Most things are straightforward, but there are a few things to note:
A declaration is a variable or a collection of variables that are used in the rules.
A rule is a transition from one state to another

html:ul.html:li: Each rule can optionally have an initial condition required to be fired
We can easily define rules for all the processors or collection of n things with ruleset.
For our use case, rules are used to define

html:ol.html:li: Controller actions
Receiving a request from the network
Retrying stalled requests

fr:mainmatter.html:p: A startstate is the intial configuration for all our declarations.
An invariant is something that Murphi checks to ensure is true at all possible configurations of the system.

html:ol.html:li: Find all rules whose conditions are true in the current state. (i.e. conditional expressions are true, given the current values of the global variables).
Choose one arbitrarily and execute the action, yielding a new state.

fr:title.text: Why three virtual channels

fr:mainmatter.html:p: The valid-invalid protocol shipped with the Murphi docs uses two Virtual Channels. A directory protocol needs three: one each for requests, forwarded requests, and responses. The reason is that deadlock is a cycle in the dependency graph, so it suffices to exhibit one.

html:ul.html:li: A node issues GetS to the directory, giving an edge N_1 \to D.
The directory forwards Fwd-GetS to the owner, extending the chain to N_1 \to D \to N_2.
The owner sends data back to the requester, closing the cycle N_1 \to D \to N_2 \to N_1.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: The data closing that cycle would travel on the same channel as the requests waiting behind it, so a full request buffer wedges the response that would drain it. Partitioning by message class breaks the cycle:

html:ul.html:li: Request: GetS, GetM, PutS, PutM
Forwarded: Fwd-GetS, Fwd-GetM, Inv, PutAck
Response: Data, InvAck

fr:mainmatter.html:p: These are enumerated directly in the model's MessageType.

fr:title.text: Losing data to a PutM/Fwd-GetM race

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Losing data to a PutM/Fwd-GetM race

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Consider the PutM rule that downgrades a cache from modified to invalid. The evicting cache must not drop the data when it sends PutM, because it may still have to service a forwarded request; it transitions to MI^A and keeps the value. But nothing stops the PutAck from arriving first, taking it to I before the Fwd-GetM shows up. The data is gone and the forwarded request has nobody to answer it.

Fix. Add the M^D state to the directory controller. While in M^D, a PutM from a node that is not the current owner stalls until the data arrives. Leaving M^D for M requires the new owner to send data back to the directory even on a three-hop transaction, so the directory learns that the forward actually completed. I have not found a cleaner way to close this race without the extra state.

fr:title.text: Deadlocking two stores against a load

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Deadlocking two stores against a load

fr:mainmatter.html:p: The M^D fix introduces a deadlock of its own. Take two processors that store-miss and a third that load-misses. The second store wins at the directory: the first store gets data and moves IM^{AD} \to IM^{A}, then the second triggers a Fwd-GetM that takes ownership away from it.

Meanwhile the load miss sits in IS^D. When its Inv arrives, the table says to stall — and because Inv and Fwd-GetM share the forwarded channel, that stall blocks the Fwd-GetM behind it. The winning processor never receives the data, and nothing ever drains the channel.

Fix. Another transient state absent from the table: II^A, meaning "was in IS^A, got invalidated, now waiting on PutAck before settling in I". The invalidation is processed rather than stalled, so the forwarded channel keeps moving.

fr:title.text: Not clearing the owner too eagerly

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Not clearing the owner too eagerly

fr:mainmatter.html:p: One more correction to the table: when the home directory is in M and receives a GetS, it must not clear the owner field as the figure directs. Once in S^D, the directory can no longer tell whether an incoming PutM came from the owner (and should stall) or from a stale node. The owner is only cleared once the data has actually arrived.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: The first processor issues GetS and waits in IS^D, while the home directory has already moved to E and sent it ExclusiveData. A second processor then issues GetM, and home's Fwd-GetM overtakes the data in flight.

fr:title.text: Losing exclusive data to an invalidation

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Losing exclusive data to an invalidation

fr:mainmatter.html:p: The nastier version of the same race: the invalidation arrives before the forward. By the II^A rule inherited from MSI, a PutAck in that state drops the line to I. This discards data a forwarded request is about to ask for.

html:ol.html:li: Proc_1 load-misses → IS^D

Proc_2 issues GetM → IM^{AD}
Home sends Inv to Proc_1
Home forwards Fwd-GetM to Proc_1
Proc_1 receives Inv → II^D
Proc_1 receives ExclusiveData → I, and the data is lost

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Fix. ExclusiveData pays for itself a second time. Because the message is distinguishable from ordinary Data, a cache receiving it in II^D knows it was the first reader and transitions to E instead of I. There, the pending Fwd-GetM or Fwd-GetS is handled correctly.
